..
Issued at 220 AM CDT Sun Oct 11 2026

Mid-level ridging remains present across the Central Plains  
with a high amplitude trough over the western CONUS and the 
remnants of Hurricane Isaias merging into the synoptic pattern 
as a shortwave over the eastern CONUS. The shortwave will 
continue to lift north and merge with the flow today, which will
further amplify the ridging over the Central Plains. At the 
surface, a stationary front is draped from southern Ontario to 
SD where lee cyclogenesis occurred yesterday. High pressure is 
present over the Gulf Coast, southeast of the low associated 
with Isaias, leaving the Central Plains sandwiched between the 
low in SD and high pressure to the southeast. This has resulted 
in southerly surface flow across the area, which combined with 
the mid-level ridging, will continue to support temperatures 
15-20 degrees above normal. Highs today and Monday will be in 
the upper 80s and low 90s, which will approach, if not break, 
record highs. Also of note, low temperatures tonight and Monday 
night will only fall into the upper 60s and low 70s, which is in
line with record high minimum temperatures.

Tonight into Monday, a shortwave will move through the flow,  
inciting lee cyclogenesis in northeast CO. This low pressure 
system will lift across NE through the day, tightening the 
pressure gradient over the Central Plains, as high pressure 
remains in place over the Gulf Coast. This will result in a 
breezy day on Monday, with sustained winds expected to be in the
15-20 mph range with gusts up to 35 mph possible. Ordinarily, 
this would raise fire weather concerns during this time of year,
and while it has been very dry for the last week or so, 
afternoon RH values will only drop to 35-45%, so Red Flag 
conditions are not expected to be met. However, this is 
something that bears watching over the next couple of forecast 
cycles.

As the low pressure system continues to move northeast, it will 
push a cold front across NE and IA Monday evening/overnight. 
This front is expected to advance into northern MO Tuesday 
morning before stalling out. How far south the front makes it 
before stalling will dictate how hot temperatures will be across
the area. North of the front, highs will likely be capped in 
the upper 70s and low 80s, while areas south of the front will 
experience another day of highs pushing towards or above 90F.

Precipitation chances (25-35%) will add another wrinkle in how 
high temperatures will climb Tuesday afternoon. Moisture 
transport from the Gulf is expected to reach the area on Tuesday 
and lift along the slow moving front may be enough to induce 
showers and storms Tuesday afternoon/evening. Currently, model 
guidance suggests that Tuesday afternoon will remain mostly dry 
before shower and storm chances increase (60-80%) Tuesday 
evening into the overnight hours as a 30 kt LLJ noses into the 
area. With PWAT values forecast to be in 2-2.25" range, heavy 
rainfall is on the table, though the finer details of this setup
still need to be ironed out.

Forecast uncertainty increases Wednesday as model solutions 
diverge regarding the handling of the front across northern MO. 
The deterministic GFS and GEFS indicate that the front will 
continue moving south through the day on Wednesday, while the 
Canadian, ECMWF, and ENS hold the front around the I-70 
corridor. This discrepancy is important, as areas along and 
south of the front will see 500-1000 J/kg of MUCAPE develop 
Wednesday afternoon in conjunction with 40-50 kts of deep layer 
shear, creating a low CAPE, high shear setup for potentially 
strong to severe storms. However, given the uncertainty on the 
placement of the front, it is difficult to say where the most 
favorable location for storms is Wednesday afternoon/evening. 
Heavy rainfall also remains possible, particularly along the 
front, Wednesday into Thursday.

Models continue to diverge through the end of the forecast 
period, with the GFS, Canadian, and GEFS lifting the western 
CONUS trough into the flow and pushing another cold front across 
the Central Plains, while the ECMWF and ENS generate a cutoff 
low over the western CONUS and indicate that mid-level ridging 
will remain present over the central CONUS. However, regardless 
of which solution you chose to look at, with the initial cold 
frontal passage on Tuesday/Wednesday, temperatures through the 
end of the forecast period should return to near seasonal values
with highs in the 60s and low 70s behind the front.
